lead: Two pushdown automata can have the same states, the same stack and the same accepted language, yet differ in one thing: choice. A nondeterministic PDA may branch at a step and accept if any branch survives. A deterministic PDA has at most one move at every step, so each input has at most one run. That single restriction shrinks the family of accepted languages. It also buys two things programmers want: fast parsing in time proportional to input length, and closure under complement.
prereq: You need the machine and its instantaneous descriptions from 4.1 and the two acceptance conventions from 4.2.

blocks.text: In 4.1 the transition function δ takes a state, an input symbol and the stack top, and returns a set of moves. That set may hold zero, one or many moves. When it holds several, or when the machine can also move on ε, one input string gets several runs, and the machine accepts if any run accepts. That is the ordinary pushdown automaton. It is now called an NPDA, a nondeterministic pushdown automaton.
A DPDA, a deterministic pushdown automaton, is an NPDA with two extra rules.
|δ(q, a, X)| ≤ 1 for every a in Σ ∪ {ε}   and   δ(q, ε, X) ≠ ∅  →  δ(q, a, X) = ∅ for every a in Σ
blocks.where: q is a state; a is an input symbol or ε; Σ is the input alphabet; X is the stack top; ε is the empty input (a silent move); δ(q, a, X) is the set of moves for that triple; |·| is the size of the set.

blocks.text: Rule 1 caps every set at one move. Rule 2 closes the other door: if the machine can move on ε with stack top X in state q, it may not read any input symbol with that same q and X. Rule 2 is the part students forget. Without it the machine could either read the next symbol or pop silently from the same configuration, and those are two runs. Two runs is choice.
A DFA is already a DPDA: it never changes the stack and never moves on ε. A DPDA is much stronger than a DFA, because the stack still holds an unbounded amount of information.

sections.h3: Three facts and the DCFL family

blocks.text: Three results tie the two machines together.

items: Fact 1: NPDAs accept exactly the context-free languages. 4.4 proves both directions.
Fact 2: every DPDA is an NPDA, so every language a DPDA accepts is a context-free language.
Fact 3: some context-free languages are accepted by no DPDA. The standard witness is L = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1} ∪ {aⁿb²ⁿ : n ≥ 1}.

blocks.text: Name the smaller family the deterministic context-free languages, DCFL. The chain regular ⊂ DCFL ⊂ CFL is strict at both steps: {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1} is a DCFL but not regular, and the union L above is a CFL but not a DCFL.

Complement. DCFLs are closed under complement. The swap of final and non-final states is only correct on a machine that never stops before the end of the input, so normalise first. Add a non-final state that consumes the rest of the input while popping the stack; any run that would have got stuck now finishes there and rejects. Now every run reads the whole input, so swapping final and non-final states accepts exactly the strings the original rejects. The same swap fails for an NPDA: one string can have an accepting run and a rejecting run at once, so flipping final states says nothing. Context-free languages are indeed not closed under complement (see Unit 3, Closure properties of context-free languages).

Linear-time parsing. A DPDA reads the input left to right and does a fixed amount of work per move. On a string of length n the run has O(n) moves, so recognition takes time proportional to n. Compilers live on this. A top-down or bottom-up parser (4.5) is a DPDA when the grammar permits it. When the grammar forces backtracking, the parser needs the full NPDA and can slow down badly.

figure.caption: Each ring holds one language. The chain regular ⊂ DCFL ⊂ CFL is strict at both steps, so the union of the two a-b languages sits outside the deterministic ring.

spec.aria: Three nested regions: the outermost holds all context-free languages and one language that is not deterministic, inside it the deterministic ones, and inside those the regular languages.

examples.question: Build a DPDA with final state q₂ for L₁ = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1}, check it against both determinism rules, and explain why no DPDA accepts L₁ ∪ L₂ where L₂ = {aⁿb²ⁿ : n ≥ 1}.
steps: Take stack alphabet Γ = {A, Z₀}, with Z₀ the bottom marker. States are q₀ (reading a's), q₁ (reading b's) and q₂ (final). Start state q₀.
Transitions: δ(q₀,a,Z₀) = (q₀,AZ₀); δ(q₀,a,A) = (q₀,AA); δ(q₀,b,A) = (q₁,ε); δ(q₁,b,A) = (q₁,ε); δ(q₁,ε,Z₀) = (q₂,Z₀). Every other triple has no move.
Rule 1: each of the five entries is a single move, and all other sets are empty. All sets have size 0 or 1.

Rule 2: the only ε-entry is at (q₁, Z₀). No input row exists for (q₁, Z₀), so there is no clash. At (q₁, A) the input row δ(q₁,b,A) exists, and δ(q₁,ε,A) is empty. Both rules hold, so the machine is deterministic.
Move count on aⁿbⁿ: n push moves, n pop moves, one ε-move, so 2n+1 moves. For n = 3 that is 3 + 3 + 1 = 7 moves.

Now add L₂ = {aⁿb²ⁿ : n ≥ 1}. On the prefix aⁿb the two languages agree. To finish aⁿbⁿ the machine pops one A per b; to finish aⁿb²ⁿ it pops one A per two b's. Both choices need the same input prefix aⁿb, so at the first b the machine must already know which case it is in.

Knowing without reading is a guess. A DPDA has at most one move per triple and no ε-move beside an input move, so it cannot guess. Therefore no DPDA accepts L₁ ∪ L₂. The union is still a CFL, being the union of two CFLs, so it is a CFL that is not a DCFL.
examples.answer: The DPDA above accepts {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1}, makes 2n+1 moves (7 moves for n = 3) and satisfies both determinism rules; the union with {aⁿb²ⁿ : n ≥ 1} forces a guess at the first b, so no DPDA accepts it.
examples.check:
n = 3
push_moves = 1 + (n - 1)   # first a uses the Z0 row, the rest use the A row
pop_moves = 1 + (n - 1)    # first b in q0, the rest in q1
eps_moves = 1              # the silent move to q2
total = push_moves + pop_moves + eps_moves
print(push_moves)
print(pop_moves)
print(total)

traps: A short transition table is not a proof of determinism. Check both clauses: at most one entry per (q, a, X), and no ε-move beside an input move for the same (q, X).
An ε-row is not harmless. Once δ(q, ε, X) is non-empty, every input row for that same (q, X) must be emptied, or the machine is nondeterministic.
Do not assume every CFL has a DPDA. {aⁿbⁿ} ∪ {aⁿb²ⁿ} is context-free and provably has no DPDA; examiners like this counterexample.
For DPDAs, acceptance by empty stack is weaker than acceptance by final state. The two conventions matched in 4.2 for NPDAs; they do not match here, so state which one you use.

quiz.q: State the two conditions that make a pushdown automaton deterministic.
quiz.a: At most one move per (state, input symbol, stack top): |δ(q,a,X)| ≤ 1. And if δ(q,ε,X) is non-empty, then δ(q,a,X) must be empty for every input symbol a.

quiz.q: Why does an ε-move sitting beside an input move for the same (q, X) destroy determinism, even when each row holds only one move?
quiz.a: From the same configuration the machine can either read the next symbol or pop silently. Those lead to different configurations on the same input, so the run branches. Two runs means choice, which a DPDA forbids.

quiz.q: Is every DFA a DPDA? Is every DPDA a DFA? Answer with one reason each.
quiz.a: Every DFA is a DPDA: keep the stack unchanged, never take an ε-move, and each (q, a, X) has at most one move. Not every DPDA is a DFA: {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1} needs the stack and is not regular.

quiz.q: L₁ = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1} is a DCFL. Show in three lines why L₁ ∪ {aⁿb²ⁿ : n ≥ 1} is not.
quiz.a: Both parts share the prefix aⁿb. Finishing the first part needs one pop per b; finishing the second needs one pop per two b's. The first b is the decision point and the input seen so far is identical in both cases, so a deterministic machine would have to guess. So no DPDA accepts the union.

quiz.q: DCFLs are closed under complement but CFLs are not. Explain the difference using runs.
quiz.a: A DPDA has at most one run per input, so swapping final and non-final states (after rewriting the machine so that every run reads the whole input) flips exactly one verdict. An NPDA can have an accepting run and a non-accepting run for the same string, so swapping final states does not produce the complement.

quiz.q: Why does a DPDA recognise a string of length n in time proportional to n, while an NPDA may not?
quiz.a: The DPDA has one run, and each move reads at most one symbol and does constant stack work, so the run has O(n) moves. The NPDA may explore many branches, so the number of moves can grow much faster than n.

beyond: Not for the exam. Deterministic pushdown automata are the theory behind the parsers in real compilers: the LR(1) family generates exactly the deterministic context-free languages, while the LL and LALR(1) parsers used in practice cover proper subclasses of them. A conflict means the grammar is not in that tool's class, so a different (still deterministic) grammar or a stronger parser is needed; it does not by itself prove the language is not a DCFL. Practical data formats such as JSON are designed so a single-pass deterministic parser reads them without backtracking. Search next for deterministic context-free grammar, LR(1) parsing, and the DPDA complement construction.
